nodes.body:

FLELMR CODE: 1160

nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name:  Atlantic menhaden
Scientific Name:  Brevoortia tyrannus

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum: Chordata
      Class:  Osteichthyes
      Order: Clupeiformes
      Family:  Clupeidae

nodes.title: Synonyms
nodes.body:
Other Common Names:  Bunker, Pogy, Fatback  (2303)

Other:	Reference for Scientific Name (Latrobe 1802)
	Reference for Classification (1914)

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  Atlantic menhaden fishery is one of the largest fisheries in the world (2303; 2319).  The fish is used for meal, oil, cattle and poultry feeds and in commercial products (2315). Captured in a gillnet fishery in the Indian River Lagoon (2317).

Recreational:  Caught and used as bait.

Ecological Role:  Clupeids represent one of the greatest sources of harvestable live animal protein in tropical seas, the biology of these fishes is important (2313).  Brevoortia tyrannus is an important trophic link as a prey source for many fish, avian and marine mammal predators.   Brevoortia tyrannus is known to frequently hybridize with Brevoortia smithi thus B. tyrannus x smithi is common to abundant in the Indian River lagoon. (2300; 848, 1988; 2320)

Indicator:  The appearance of Ulcerative Disease Syndrome (UDS) in Atlantic menhaden can be an indicator of bacterial/fungal/anthropogenic pathogens present in the ecosystem (2310; 2314).  Atlantic menhaden can be utilized as an assay for surface film toxicity tests for various compounds such as, chlorinated compounds, Tributyltin (TBT) and other toxic compounds (2302).

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  Nova Scotia to Jupiter Inlet, Florida (2318, 2317; 2300; 2304) and in Everglades National Park (2309; 2304).

Within Study Area:  Northern Indian River to Jupiter Inlet (1814; 2317; 887; 848, 993; 2320).

Life Mode:  Estuarine and neritic schooling filter-feeding omnivore.

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body:
Type:  Adults occur near the surface in shallow continental shelf waters.  Larvae are pelagic in neritic and estuarine waters  (2304). In the Indian River Lagoon found in open lagoon waters (2320) over seagrass, sand bottom  and  freshwater tributaries (848, 1988).   Juveniles  inhabit estuaries for the first year and then move to coastal waters (2316).

Substrate: Near surface waters of estuaries and coastal waters though detritus and microorganismal films may be taken during feeding off rocks, vegetation and sediment substrates (2312).

Physical/chemical:  Found in water temperatures ranging from 0-34 �C, with a preference for 15-25 oC water (2307; 2304; 2302).    Temperature above 33 �C can cause death in young (2311).   Found in all salinities up to 38 ppt (2307).   Larvae grow faster in low salinities, 5-10 ppt (2306).  Larvae and juveniles prefer lower salinities than the adults (2304).

Movements and Migrations:  The Atlantic menhaden population consists of at least two component populations. The adult population over-winters  in offshore waters south of  Cape Hatteras, North Carolina. The northern component of the population then moves north during the spring, with the older members of the population moving the furthest north.  In the fall the northern population moves south again.  The southern component remains south of Cape Hatteras and does not migrate north and south on such a grand scale but, moves inshore and offshore seasonally.  The juveniles along the Atlantic coast remain in the nursery areas of the estuaries and do not migrate the first year (2315).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode:  Gonochoristic, polygamous, oviparous, iteroparous.

Mating and Spawning:  Spawning varies in relation to geographic location, Northern Atlantic populations spawn  during the summer, Mid-Atlantic populations spring and fall, southern Atlantic populations spawn during the winter (2308; 2303; 2305).  B. tyrannus spawns within the Indian River Lagoon   December-March (1814; 2300).

Fecundity:  Fecundity increases with length, with a range of 38,000 (203 mm) to 561,000 (346 mm) ova (2305).

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg:   Pelagic, transparent, spherical, ranging from 1.4 to 1.95 mm in diameter with a single oil globule (2308; 2301).  Eggs hatch in 48- 54 hrs (2308; 2304).
Larvae:  Larvae are 4.5-5.0 mm in length at hatching (2308; 2304).  Larvae grow faster in low salinities, 5-10 ppt (2306).  Temperatures above 33 oC can cause death in young (2311).
Juvenile:  Reaches juvenile stage at 30-41 mm (2308; 2304).  Larvae found in temperatures ranging from 0-25 oC preferring 15-20 oC water (2307). Temperatures above 33 oC can cause death in young (2311).  Juveniles found in estuaries (1814; 2317; 887; 993).
Adult:  Maturity can be reached as early as age 1 (180-280 mm FL) but, all reach maturity by age 3 (over 200 mm FL) (2305; 2303).   Adults can reach 500 mm (2303; 2300).

nodes.title: Trophic Modes
nodes.body: Eating: Feeds on small organism strained from the water.  Items found in stomach include; crustaceans, copepods, unicellular plants along with a large percentage of  mud and debris (2303).  Recent studies have shown the Atlantic menhaden should be classified as an omnivorous microphagous filter- feeding fish, since amorphous matter (mud and debris) makes up a large portion of the diet (2312).

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body:
Predation:  Most predatory fish, birds and marine mammals prey upon menhaden (2303).  Also a major source of energy movement from estuary to adjacent continental shelf.

Factors influencing populations:  Temperature for developing young, loss of estuarine nursery habitat, heavy natural predation and over fishing.

sections.heading: TAXONOMY
sections.content:
Common Name:  Atlantic menhaden
Scientific Name:  Brevoortia tyrannus

sections.heading: Classification
sections.content:
Phylum: Chordata
      Class:  Osteichthyes
      Order: Clupeiformes
      Family:  Clupeidae

sections.heading: Synonyms
sections.content:
Other Common Names:  Bunker, Pogy, Fatback  (2303)

Other:	Reference for Scientific Name (Latrobe 1802)
	Reference for Classification (1914)

sections.heading: VALUE & STATUS
sections.content:
Commercial:  Atlantic menhaden fishery is one of the largest fisheries in the world (2303; 2319).  The fish is used for meal, oil, cattle and poultry feeds and in commercial products (2315). Captured in a gillnet fishery in the Indian River Lagoon (2317).

Recreational:  Caught and used as bait.

Ecological Role:  Clupeids represent one of the greatest sources of harvestable live animal protein in tropical seas, the biology of these fishes is important (2313).  Brevoortia tyrannus is an important trophic link as a prey source for many fish, avian and marine mammal predators.   Brevoortia tyrannus is known to frequently hybridize with Brevoortia smithi thus B. tyrannus x smithi is common to abundant in the Indian River lagoon. (2300; 848, 1988; 2320)

Indicator:  The appearance of Ulcerative Disease Syndrome (UDS) in Atlantic menhaden can be an indicator of bacterial/fungal/anthropogenic pathogens present in the ecosystem (2310; 2314).  Atlantic menhaden can be utilized as an assay for surface film toxicity tests for various compounds such as, chlorinated compounds, Tributyltin (TBT) and other toxic compounds (2302).

sections.heading: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
sections.content:
Overall:  Nova Scotia to Jupiter Inlet, Florida (2318, 2317; 2300; 2304) and in Everglades National Park (2309; 2304).

Within Study Area:  Northern Indian River to Jupiter Inlet (1814; 2317; 887; 848, 993; 2320).

Life Mode:  Estuarine and neritic schooling filter-feeding omnivore.

sections.heading: BENTHIC HABITAT
sections.content:
Type:  Adults occur near the surface in shallow continental shelf waters.  Larvae are pelagic in neritic and estuarine waters  (2304). In the Indian River Lagoon found in open lagoon waters (2320) over seagrass, sand bottom  and  freshwater tributaries (848, 1988).   Juveniles  inhabit estuaries for the first year and then move to coastal waters (2316).

Substrate: Near surface waters of estuaries and coastal waters though detritus and microorganismal films may be taken during feeding off rocks, vegetation and sediment substrates (2312).

Physical/chemical:  Found in water temperatures ranging from 0-34 �C, with a preference for 15-25 oC water (2307; 2304; 2302).    Temperature above 33 �C can cause death in young (2311).   Found in all salinities up to 38 ppt (2307).   Larvae grow faster in low salinities, 5-10 ppt (2306).  Larvae and juveniles prefer lower salinities than the adults (2304).

Movements and Migrations:  The Atlantic menhaden population consists of at least two component populations. The adult population over-winters  in offshore waters south of  Cape Hatteras, North Carolina. The northern component of the population then moves north during the spring, with the older members of the population moving the furthest north.  In the fall the northern population moves south again.  The southern component remains south of Cape Hatteras and does not migrate north and south on such a grand scale but, moves inshore and offshore seasonally.  The juveniles along the Atlantic coast remain in the nursery areas of the estuaries and do not migrate the first year (2315).

sections.heading: REPRODUCTION
sections.content:
Reproductive Mode:  Gonochoristic, polygamous, oviparous, iteroparous.

Mating and Spawning:  Spawning varies in relation to geographic location, Northern Atlantic populations spawn  during the summer, Mid-Atlantic populations spring and fall, southern Atlantic populations spawn during the winter (2308; 2303; 2305).  B. tyrannus spawns within the Indian River Lagoon   December-March (1814; 2300).

Fecundity:  Fecundity increases with length, with a range of 38,000 (203 mm) to 561,000 (346 mm) ova (2305).

sections.heading: Length Range
sections.content:
Egg:   Pelagic, transparent, spherical, ranging from 1.4 to 1.95 mm in diameter with a single oil globule (2308; 2301).  Eggs hatch in 48- 54 hrs (2308; 2304).
Larvae:  Larvae are 4.5-5.0 mm in length at hatching (2308; 2304).  Larvae grow faster in low salinities, 5-10 ppt (2306).  Temperatures above 33 oC can cause death in young (2311).
Juvenile:  Reaches juvenile stage at 30-41 mm (2308; 2304).  Larvae found in temperatures ranging from 0-25 oC preferring 15-20 oC water (2307). Temperatures above 33 oC can cause death in young (2311).  Juveniles found in estuaries (1814; 2317; 887; 993).
Adult:  Maturity can be reached as early as age 1 (180-280 mm FL) but, all reach maturity by age 3 (over 200 mm FL) (2305; 2303).   Adults can reach 500 mm (2303; 2300).

sections.heading: Trophic Modes
sections.content: Eating: Feeds on small organism strained from the water.  Items found in stomach include; crustaceans, copepods, unicellular plants along with a large percentage of  mud and debris (2303).  Recent studies have shown the Atlantic menhaden should be classified as an omnivorous microphagous filter- feeding fish, since amorphous matter (mud and debris) makes up a large portion of the diet (2312).

sections.heading: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
sections.content:
Predation:  Most predatory fish, birds and marine mammals prey upon menhaden (2303).  Also a major source of energy movement from estuary to adjacent continental shelf.

Factors influencing populations:  Temperature for developing young, loss of estuarine nursery habitat, heavy natural predation and over fishing.
